title: The Island in the Loire to the Grave at Amiens: the Saint-Michel, the Voyages Extraordinaires, and a Man Who Mostly Read His Way Around the World
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Île Feydeau, the house on the made ground
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Jules Gabriel Verne is born on the eighth of February in his grandmother's house at No. 4 rue Olivier-de-Clisson, on the Île Feydeau, a slab of made ground dropped into the Loire and built over with the stone mansions of shipowners. His mother's people are shipping people; his father is a lawyer from Provins. Nantes has grown rich on sugar and, within living memory, on the slave ships, and the island itself settles and tilts under its own weight, so that the doorframes go crooked. From the upper windows a child sees masts moving where a street should be.
sources: Musee Jules Verne de Nantes, biographical highlights
suggested_refs: The stone houses of the Ile Feydeau, Nantes, and the plaque at 4 rue Olivier-de-Clisson

stops.name: Nantes, the removals of the Verne family
stops.date_confidence: each address attested; the date is the first move, and the sequence runs to 1842
stops.campa: The family moves and moves again inside one city: quai Jean-Bart in 1829, the year his brother Paul is born; a boarding school on the place du Bouffay in 1834; a summer house at Chantenay on the hill above the river from 1836; rue Jean-Jacques-Rousseau in 1840; the Petit Seminaire de Saint-Donatien in 1842, the year his sister Marie arrives. Four centuries before, this same town tried Gilles de Rais in two courts and burned him by the river, and Arthurian romance sets the death of Ither before Nantes. The boy learns the city as a list of addresses and the sea as a rumour at the end of them.
suggested_refs: The quai Jean-Bart and the place du Bouffay, Nantes, as they stood before the Loire arms were filled in

stops.name: Paimboeuf, the boy taken off the Coralie
stops.date_confidence: tradition only; the story is a reconstruction popularised by his grand-niece Marguerite Allotte de la Fuye in 1928 and treated by later scholarship as exaggerated or invented
stops.campa: By the account his grand-niece Marguerite Allotte de la Fuye publishes in 1928, the eleven-year-old signs on as cabin boy aboard the three-master Coralie, bound for the Indies, meaning to bring his cousin Caroline a coral necklace. His father Pierre takes the steamer down the estuary and lifts him off at Paimboeuf before the ship clears the river, and extracts from him a promise to travel from then on only in imagination. Modern scholarship does not believe a word of it. The story stands here where the biography put it, with the doubt kept beside it.
sources: Marguerite Allotte de la Fuye, Jules Verne, sa vie, son oeuvre (1928)
Wikipedia, 'Jules Verne', citing later biographical scholarship
suggested_refs: The quays of Paimboeuf, deep-water outport of Nantes before the Loire was dredged

stops.name: Lycee Royal de Nantes, the average pupil
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of enrolment
stops.campa: He enters the Lycee Royal, later the Lycee Georges-Clemenceau, on the rue Malherbe. Masters record a boy strong in geography and in Latin verse and restless in everything else. His brother Paul is being fitted for the navy and will get the sea; Jules is being fitted for his father's practice and will get the law. Between the two futures he writes verses and reads voyages, and the geography prize is the only one that ever looks like a prophecy. Nantes is at this moment losing its deep-water trade to the silting of the Loire, and the masts he grew up among are thinning out year by year.
sources: Musee Jules Verne de Nantes, biographical highlights
suggested_refs: The Lycee Georges-Clemenceau, rue Malherbe, Nantes, formerly the Lycee Royal

stops.name: Rennes, the baccalaureat
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He sits his baccalaureat at Rennes on the twenty-ninth of July and is graded Assez Bien, Good Enough. It is the exact temperature of his father's expectations: the boy will do, the boy will pass, the boy will go to Paris and read law and come home to the practice on the quay. Rennes is the nearest thing to a foreign city he has seen, a day's road east and an examination hall where the certificate is signed by strangers. He goes to Paris and reads law. He never comes home, and the practice on the quay passes to somebody else.
suggested_refs: The examination registers of the Academie de Rennes, July 1846

segments.name: Paris: the Law and the Boulevard

stops.name: Latin Quarter, the law student after the barricades
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; he arrives after the February overthrow and after the June Days, not during them
stops.campa: He takes lodgings in the Latin Quarter to read law. He arrives in July, which is to say afterwards: Louis-Philippe has already gone, the June rising has already been shot off the streets, and what Verne walks through is the smell of a revolution rather than the event. In December the city elects Louis-Napoleon. Verne attends salons instead of lectures, writes tragedies nobody wants, and lives on an allowance calculated by a notary in Nantes for a young man who is doing what he was told.
suggested_refs: The student lodgings of the rue de l'Ancienne-Comedie quarter, Paris, 1848

stops.name: Theatre Historique, Les Pailles rompues
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twelfth of June his one-act comedy Les Pailles rompues is staged on the Boulevard du Temple, at the theatre Alexandre Dumas built for himself. Verne has met the father and befriended the son, and the son has pushed the piece through. It runs, it is liked well enough, and it settles nothing: he is now a playwright who is also a law student, in a city with more of both than it needs. He sends his father the reviews and asks for another year.
suggested_refs: The Theatre Historique on the Boulevard du Temple, Paris, Dumas's own house

stops.name: Paris, the licence in law and the Musee des familles
stops.date_confidence: the degree is attested to January 1851; the stories are dated by the issues that carried them
stops.campa: He takes the licence en droit in January and never practises. In July and August the Musee des familles, edited by Pitre-Chevalier, prints his first two stories, Les Premiers navires de la marine mexicaine and Un voyage en ballon, and the shape of everything after is already visible: a real vehicle, a real instrument list, a route that can be checked. Martin Paz and Les Chateaux en Californie follow in 1852, the year he takes the secretary's desk at the Theatre Lyrique and founds a bachelors' club called the Onze-sans-femme. Maitre Zacharius runs in 1854, Un hivernage dans les glaces in 1855.
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Un hivernage dans les glaces' (which dates it to March-April 1855, against the English article)
suggested_refs: Bound volumes of the Musee des familles, 1851-1855

stops.name: Amiens, the wedding of Auguste Lelarge
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: He comes north to stand as best man at his friend Lelarge's wedding and meets the bride's sister: Honorine Anne Hebee Morel, a widow of twenty-six with two small daughters. He is twenty-eight and has nothing but a desk at a theatre. Amiens is a cathedral town on the Somme that will hold him for the last thirty-four years of his life, elect him to its council, and bury him. Marcel Proust will translate Ruskin's Bible of Amiens here, and Gilles Deleuze will take his first teaching post at its lycee. Verne has come for a wedding and found a town.
suggested_refs: Amiens cathedral and the Somme quarters of Saint-Leu, 1856

stops.name: Paris, marriage to Honorine Morel
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the church or mairie of the ceremony is named in no source reached
stops.campa: They marry on the tenth of January. The date is fixed and the city is fixed; the room is not, and no source consulted names the church or the mairie, an unlit window at the centre of the marriage. Honorine brings two stepdaughters and a family of brokers, and it is her brother who arranges the position that will pay for the writing. Verne acquires, in one January, a wife, a household, a trade he does not want, and the working hours that will produce sixty novels.
suggested_refs: Parisian marriage registers of January 1857 (not located)

stops.name: Palais Brongniart, the stockbroker's hours
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; he keeps the trade until about 1862
stops.campa: He takes a place as agent de change on the floor of the Bourse with an associate named Fernand Eggly. Colleagues remember a man who writes before dawn, arrives with ink on his fingers, and talks about balloons. For five years the account books and the manuscripts run in parallel columns, and the discipline of the second is paid for by the boredom of the first. Nothing in the Voyages extraordinaires will ever be free: every airship and submarine in them is costed, provisioned, and paid for by somebody, in figures.
suggested_refs: The trading floor of the Palais Brongniart, Paris, under the Second Empire

stops.name: Bordeaux, the free passage south before going north
stops.date_confidence: attested by Ian Thompson; English Wikipedia's 'July 1858' is contradicted by its own article on Backwards to Britain and is not followed here
stops.campa: Aristide Hignard's brother is a shipping agent and offers the composer and his friend a free passage. To reach Scotland they must first go the wrong way, down to Bordeaux, and take the SS Hamburg from there: the roundabout route that gives the book Verne writes about it its title, Voyage a reculons en Angleterre et en Ecosse. He is thirty-one and has never left France. The account he keeps is a novelist's rehearsal, a real journey written as though it were invented, and Hetzel will refuse it.
suggested_refs: The Bordeaux quays and the SS Hamburg, August 1859

stops.name: Liverpool, the first foreign port
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by Thompson
stops.campa: They land at Liverpool on the twenty-fifth. A shipowner's grandson from Nantes stands on the Mersey and counts the traffic: docks running for miles, iron hulls, coal smoke, a scale of shipping that his own river has never carried. He looks at British engineering the way a man looks at a rival family's house. Eight years later he will come back to this water to board the largest ship in the world, and in between he will write the ships he wants rather than the ones that exist.
sources: Ian Thompson, Jules Verne's Scotland (via Undiscovered Scotland review)
suggested_refs: The Mersey dock system at Liverpool, 1859

stops.name: Edinburgh, the city that becomes a stock of scenery
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by Thompson: arrival by train from Liverpool, late evening
stops.campa: He reaches Edinburgh late on the twenty-sixth by train and spends the following days in the Old Town, then Fife, Stirling, Glasgow, Loch Lomond, and the Trossachs. No foreign city will furnish more of his fiction. The coal country under Loch Katrine becomes Les Indes noires; the Hebrides and the west coast come back in Le Rayon vert; the Scottish gentleman with money and a fixed purpose becomes a whole class of his heroes. He is a tourist for three weeks and a quarryman of the place for forty years.
sources: Ian Thompson, 'Jules Verne, Geography and Scotland'
suggested_refs: The Old Town of Edinburgh and Loch Katrine, source ground for Les Indes noires

stops.name: London, the last stage of the wrong-way voyage
stops.date_confidence: attested by Verne's own account, which closes in London; the day within the month is not fixed
stops.campa: The pair come home through London: London Bridge, St Paul's, Westminster Abbey, and a Shakespeare production at the Princess's Theatre, all of it written up in the closing chapters of the Voyage a reculons. Earlier compilations flag this leg as doubtful; it is not doubtful, it is in the book. Thirteen years later Verne will start a novel in the Reform Club, a building he never entered, in a city he had crossed once, and the world will read it as an Englishman's own account of England.
suggested_refs: The Princess's Theatre, Oxford Street, London, and its 1859 Shakespeare season

stops.name: Stockholm, Gamla Stan
stops.date_confidence: attested; he is in Stockholm 7-14 July, reached by way of Hamburg, Lubeck and Ystad
stops.campa: A second free passage, and a longer road: Paris on the second of July, Hamburg and Lubeck, Ystad on the fifth, and a week in Stockholm from the seventh. Two research compilations report a contradiction here, one making Stockholm the first stop and one making it the last. There is no contradiction. Stockholm comes first, then Gothenburg, then the crossing to Norway, and the diary says so day by day. The false conflict is recorded here so that no one has to discover it twice.
suggested_refs: Gamla Stan, Stockholm, and the Gota Canal route Verne took inland

stops.name: Christiania, across the Skagerrak
stops.date_confidence: attested; Gothenburg 17 July, Stavern 18 July, Christiania 19 July
stops.campa: From Gothenburg on the seventeenth they take the Norwegian paddle steamer Viken, eleven hours of heavy water across the Skagerrak, and land at Stavern on the Vestfold coast on the eighteenth. On the nineteenth Verne is in Christiania, and goes out from it to Sandvika and to Eidsvoll on Lake Mjosa. He is thirty-three, unpublished as a novelist, and taking notes on a country he will never set in a book: the north he uses later is the north of this fortnight, transposed.
suggested_refs: The paddle steamer Viken and the Stavern landing, July 1861

stops.name: Gaustatoppen, the summit above Rjukan
stops.date_confidence: attested to the Telemark leg of 23-30 July; the day of the climb is not separately fixed
stops.campa: He walks into Telemark, stands under the Rjukan waterfall, and climbs Gausta to the summit. It is the highest ground he will ever stand on and one of the few genuine physical exertions in a life otherwise spent at a desk or on a deck. The terrain comes back later in the Scandinavian pages of his fiction, and so does the appetite: the Verne hero is a man who goes up the mountain because the mountain has not been measured, and pays whatever the measurement costs.
stops.quote: I wanted to see what no one had yet observed, even if I had to pay for this curiosity with my life.
stops.quote_source: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea, trans. Walter James Miller and Frederick Paul Walter (Naval Institute Press); spoken by Professor Aronnax, not by Verne in his own person
suggested_refs: The Rjukanfossen waterfall and the summit of Gaustatoppen, Telemark

stops.name: Copenhagen, the race that arrives too late
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; the birth in Paris is dated 3 August 1861
stops.campa: Word reaches him in Denmark that Honorine is near her time. He leaves Hignard and runs for Paris, and on the third of August his only biological son, Michel, is born without him. Father and son will fight for twenty years; Michel will be sent to sea by court order at sixteen and shipped to India, and it is Michel who will finally handle, and rewrite, the manuscripts left when Verne dies. The son is named for the archangel; so are all three of the boats.
suggested_refs: The Copenhagen packet routes to Kiel and Hamburg, August 1861

stops.name: Paris, Hetzel and Five Weeks in a Balloon
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day of publication; the contract negotiations run through 1862
stops.campa: Alfred de Brehat sends him to Pierre-Jules Hetzel, republican, exile under the Empire, publisher of Hugo and Balzac. Hetzel reads a manuscript about a balloon crossing of Africa, tells him to cut the lecturing and add a story, and takes it. Cinq semaines en ballon appears on the thirty-first of January 1863 and sells. The first agreement is for three volumes a year at a flat fee. The Magasin d'Education et de Recreation, which popular accounts often claim he was signed to from the start, does not exist until March 1864.
suggested_refs: Hetzel's house at 18 rue Jacob, Paris, and the first edition of Cinq semaines en ballon

stops.name: Paris, Journey to the Centre of the Earth
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: The second novel goes down instead of up: a runic cryptogram, a Hamburg professor, an Icelandic crater, and a descent under the crust into a sea with its own weather. It is the book that fixes the method. Verne does not invent a world, he takes the science journals of his own decade at their word and walks a man into the consequences. The Colegio's hollow-earth thread, running through Poe and Symmes and Dante's funnel, arrives here in the one version that comes with a barometer, a chronometer, and a supply list.
stops.quote: Science, my boy, is composed of errors, but errors that it is right to make, for they lead step by step to the truth.
stops.quote_source: Journey to the Centre of the Earth, trans. William Butcher (Oxford World's Classics), p. 146
suggested_refs: Edouard Riou's illustrations for Voyage au centre de la Terre, Hetzel edition

stops.name: Paris, From the Earth to the Moon
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: A club of American artillerymen, idle after their civil war, decides to fire a projectile at the moon from Florida. The Frenchman who talks his way into the shell is called Michel Ardan, which is Nadar with the letters moved: Felix Tournachon, balloonist and photographer, who takes Mikhail Bakunin's portrait in 1862 and whose studio sits Jules Barbier's Paris in a chair under the skylight. Verne costs the shot out in tons of guncotton and gets the escape velocity nearly right, and the joke about the Gun Club is not a joke.
stops.quote: The sole preoccupation of this learned society was the destruction of humanity for philanthropic reasons and the perfection of weapons as instruments of civilization.
stops.quote_source: From the Earth to the Moon, trans. Walter James Miller (1978)
suggested_refs: Nadar's photographic studio, 35 boulevard des Capucines, and the balloon Le Geant

stops.name: Le Crotoy, the first Saint-Michel
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of the first rented villa; the Saint-Michel I is completed 29 May 1868 and bought 3 June 1868, not 1867 as English Wikipedia has it
stops.campa: He rents at Le Crotoy on the bay of the Somme in August 1865, moves to the rue Lefevre in 1866, and in the spring of 1868 into a villa called La Solitude, the year a nine-metre bourcet-malet fishing hull is finished for him and named the Saint-Michel for his son. He writes at sea. Two larger boats will follow. Four centuries earlier Joan of Arc was ferried past this same estuary as a prisoner, with a chancellor of Amiens hearing her confession on the water; Verne's desk now floats over the crossing.
suggested_refs: The villa La Solitude at Le Crotoy and the bourcet-malet rig of the Saint-Michel I

stops.name: Liverpool, boarding the largest ship in the world
stops.date_confidence: sources give both 16 and 26 March 1867 for the sailing; the disagreement is not resolved
stops.campa: With his brother Paul he boards Brunel's Great Eastern, six masts, five funnels, paddle wheels and a screw, a ship so large that no trade has yet been found that can fill her. She is running passengers to New York for the Paris Exposition season. Verne walks her decks with a notebook, measuring: this is the first machine he has ever been inside that is bigger than the ones he invents. Sources cannot agree whether she sails on the sixteenth or the twenty-sixth of the month, and no attempt is made here to settle it.
suggested_refs: The SS Great Eastern at Liverpool, 1867, and her passenger accommodation

stops.name: New York, the Manhattan piers
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Fourteen days of storm and the Great Eastern makes New York on the ninth of April. Verne's fellow passenger Adrien Marx remembers that he does not linger on Broadway: he takes the train for Niagara almost at once, as a man does who has come to see one specific thing. The crossing and the waterfront both go into Une Ville flottante, which is a novel about a ship rather than about America. It is the only time in his whole life that he touches the New World.
sources: Adrien Marx, recollection of the landing, via search summary
suggested_refs: The North River piers of Manhattan, 1867

stops.name: Niagara, the falls seen once
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; the day is not fixed in the sources reached
stops.campa: Six hundred leagues of rail to stand in front of Horseshoe Falls and watch a river fall over a cliff at a rate that can be calculated. He crosses to the Canadian side and goes behind the sheet of water. Then he turns round and goes home to a house in Picardy, and for the remaining thirty-eight years of his life he will send characters to the Congo, the pole, the moon, the sea floor, and the pampas, and go himself no further than the Mediterranean.
sources: julesverne.ca, Andrew Nash, 'Jules Verne: Signature, Niagara Falls'
suggested_refs: The Horseshoe Falls and the Table Rock walkway, 1867

stops.name: Paris, the quarrel over Captain Nemo
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of the dispute; the serial runs 20 March 1869 to 20 June 1870
stops.campa: Verne wants Nemo to be a Pole whose family the Russians killed, sinking Russian ships for revenge. Hetzel, who sells to a market and to a censor, refuses: no named empire, no named atrocity. They fight it out in letters and settle on a man with no country and no explained past, which is worse for the publisher's peace of mind and better for the book. The censor gets a captain with no named enemy, and nobody, including Verne, ever fully says what was done to him.
stops.quote: I have done with society entirely, for reasons which I alone have the right of appreciating.
stops.quote_source: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea, ch. X, public-domain English text verified against Project Gutenberg #164; spoken by Captain Nemo
suggested_refs: The Verne-Hetzel correspondence of 1869 on the character of Nemo

stops.name: Paris, the cross of the Legion of Honour
stops.date_confidence: attested for the decoration only; the same date is widely and wrongly given for the publication of Vingt mille lieues, which was serialised 1869-1870 and issued as a book that year, illustrated in November 1871
stops.campa: On the ninth of April he is made Chevalier of the Legion of Honour, proposed by a minister who reads him. The state has decided that the man writing about submarines is a national asset. Four months later the Empire that decorated him falls at Sedan, Paris is invested, and Verne, forty-two and lame in no way yet, serves in the coastguard at Le Crotoy with the Saint-Michel requisitioned under him. The Republic that emerges will name streets after him within his own lifetime.
stops.quote: We may brave human laws, but we cannot resist natural ones.
stops.quote_source: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea, Part II ch. XV, published English translation (see en.wikiquote); French original: On peut braver les lois humaines, mais non resister aux lois naturelles
suggested_refs: The 1871 illustrated Hetzel edition of Vingt mille lieues sous les mers

stops.name: Amiens, the move inland
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of the departure from Le Crotoy
stops.campa: In February he leaves the Somme bay for Amiens, his wife's town, and stays for the rest of his life. The same year he signs the twenty-year contract with Hetzel that fixes his output at two volumes annually and his income at a salary. Amiens already keeps a street and a faculty amphitheatre for Rene Just Hauy, who worked out the geometry of crystals here; it will add a boulevard, a circus, and a municipal library for Verne. He is a provincial now, on purpose, and the novels go further as the man goes less far.
suggested_refs: The Cirque Jules Verne, Amiens, opened 1889 with Verne on the council

stops.name: Paris, eighty days in Le Temps
stops.date_confidence: attested to the serialisation in Le Temps, November-December 1872; the stage version with Adolphe d'Ennery follows in 1874
stops.campa: Le Tour du monde en quatre-vingts jours runs daily in Le Temps and readers bet on the outcome; American papers wire for the ending. The circuit only closes because the Suez Canal opened in 1869, and Gustave Eiffel worked on that canal under Lesseps early in his career: an engineer's ditch makes a novelist's clock. Twenty-three years later Mark Twain, broke and paying off creditors, will run nearly the same ports for real on a lecture ticket, Sydney to Benares to London, and take rather longer than eighty days.
suggested_refs: The daily instalments of Le Tour du monde in Le Temps, autumn 1872

stops.name: Theatre du Chatelet, Michel Strogoff on stage
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day of the premiere; 1876, often given for this event, is the date of the novel, not the play
stops.campa: The stage Strogoff, written with Adolphe d'Ennery, opens at the Chatelet on the seventeenth of November and runs three hundred and eighty-six performances to November 1881. With the eighty-days spectacle of 1874, which had elephants, it makes him richer than the novels ever do. He buys bigger boats with the theatre money. The English-language biographies collapse the play into the novel's year and lose four years of a man's life; the French theatre records keep the reading date, the premiere, and the closing night.
sources: jv.gilead.org.il (cited via secondary summary; host unreachable, TLS failure)
suggested_refs: The Theatre du Chatelet playbills for Michel Strogoff, 1880-1881

segments.name: The Cruises of the Saint-Michel III

stops.name: Vigo, driven into the ria
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Saint-Michel III is a steam yacht with a crew of ten, bought with theatre money, and the first long cruise means to make Lisbon. Weather puts her into the Ria de Vigo instead, where the party, Paul Verne and Hetzel's son among them, waits four days. Verne knows this bay: he sank the Spanish treasure fleet of 1702 here in Vingt mille lieues and had Nemo salvage it to pay for his war. He is now anchored on top of his own invention, in the rain, waiting for the glass to rise.
sources: Puerto de Vigo, 'Las dos visitas de Julio Verne a Vigo'
suggested_refs: The Ria de Vigo and the wrecks of the 1702 silver fleet at Rande

stops.name: Gibraltar, the Chronicle logs the yacht
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Gibraltar Chronicle's own entry
stops.campa: The Gibraltar Chronicle enters the steam yacht Saint Michel, J. Verne owner aboard, four hours out of Tangier, clearing for Malaga, Tetuan, Oran and Algiers. It is the hardest documentary evidence of any journey he made: a harbourmaster's line of type. Lisbon and Cadiz are claimed for this leg by Spanish popular accounts and are weaker; the Chronicle names what it saw. He will come back to the Rock in 1884, the second of his two documented calls.
stops.quote: The sea doesn't belong to tyrants. On its surface they can still exercise their iniquitous claims, battle each other, devour each other, haul every earthly horror. But thirty feet below sea level, their dominion ceases, their influence fades, their power vanishes! ... Here alone lies independence! Here I recognize no superiors! Here I'm free!
stops.quote_source: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea, Part 1 ch. 10, public-domain English text as hosted on Lit2Go, translator not credited; the older Mercier Lewis version reads 'The sea does not belong to despots'
sources: Ian Thompson and Philippe Valetoux, 'Jules Verne's Visits to Gibraltar in 1878 and 1884', Verniana vol. 1
suggested_refs: The Gibraltar Chronicle shipping column, June 1878

stops.name: Algiers, the far point of the cruise
stops.date_confidence: attested to July-August 1878; the day is not fixed
stops.campa: Algiers is as far as the Saint-Michel III goes and as far as Verne ever goes: four countries in a summer, Portugal, Spain, Morocco, Algeria, all of it coastwise, none of it more than a few miles inland. His characters cross the Sahara and the pampas and the ice; their author looks at Africa from a deck and turns for home. The Mediterranean is the outer edge of the life. Everything beyond it in the sixty-odd novels comes out of the Bibliotheque nationale, the Bulletin de la Societe de geographie, and a card index.
sources: VigoE, 'Julio Verne visito Vigo... y repitio'
suggested_refs: The harbour of Algiers under the Third Republic

stops.name: Kiel, the Eider Canal a second time
stops.date_confidence: attested to 17-18 June 1881; the cruise leaves Rotterdam on 5 June
stops.campa: The Baltic cruise starts at Rotterdam on the fifth of June, runs north by Wilhelmshaven, and turns into the Eider to take the old canal through to Kiel on the seventeenth. He was last here in 1861 with Hignard, going the other way and owning nothing. Now he owns the boat, and his brother Paul is writing the voyage up for a Breton newspaper as it happens. The old canal will be superseded within fifteen years by the Kaiser Wilhelm ship canal, cut for warships.
suggested_refs: The Eiderkanal and the Holtenau lock before the 1895 Kaiser Wilhelm Canal

stops.name: Copenhagen, the voyage that gives itself a title
stops.date_confidence: reached in the second half of June; he leaves Copenhagen on 27 June and the cruise runs 3 June to 17 July. The '4 June' date in circulation is impossible, the yacht being at Rotterdam on the 5th
stops.campa: Paul Verne writes the trip up for L'Union bretonne as De Rotterdam a Copenhague, and the title fixes a cruise that in fact went further and lasted longer. They leave Copenhagen on the twenty-seventh, re-transit the Holtenau lock and the Eiderkanal, and are home by the middle of July. One account puts the yacht at Saint-Malo on the third of July, which the seventeenth-of-July end date does not comfortably allow; both dates are recorded here, neither settled.
sources: kiel-maritim.de, 'Jules Verne's Reise zum Mittelpunkt des Nordens 1881'
suggested_refs: Paul Verne's account De Rotterdam a Copenhague in L'Union bretonne, 1881

segments.name: The Amiens Years, the Grave, and After

stops.name: Amiens, rue Charles-Dubois: two shots at the gate
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Coming home in the evening of the ninth of March, Verne is shot twice at his own door by his nephew Gaston, twenty-six, who says he did it to force the French Academy to recognise his uncle. The first bullet misses. The second stays in the left leg and he limps for the remaining nineteen years. The press keeps it quiet, Gaston goes to an asylum and never comes out, and eight days later Hetzel dies. His mother Sophie dies in 1887. The books written after this are colder, and they end worse.
suggested_refs: The house at 2 rue Charles-Dubois, Amiens, Verne's residence 1882-1900

stops.name: Amiens, Hotel de Ville: the councillor
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of election; he holds the seat some fifteen years
stops.campa: He stands for the municipal council on a moderate list and is elected, and keeps the seat for fifteen years: fairs, the theatre, the tramway, the circus he helps open in 1889, the municipal library. He handles the town's cultural business the way he handles a manuscript, on time and under budget. In July 1892 he is promoted Officer of the Legion of Honour. The most travelled imagination in Europe spends its evenings on the paving and lighting committee of a cathedral town of eighty thousand.
suggested_refs: Minutes of the Amiens municipal council, 1888-1903

stops.name: Amiens, 44 boulevard Longueville: the death
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He gives up the big house on the rue Charles-Dubois in 1900 and moves to a smaller one on the boulevard Longueville, which the town will rename for him. He dies there on the twenty-fourth of March, seventy-seven years old, of chronic diabetes with a stroke, half blind, still dictating. L'Invasion de la mer is running in the Magasin as he dies, the last novel published in his lifetime; Le Phare du bout du monde comes out after, in his son Michel's hands and partly in Michel's words.
stops.quote: I have always made a point in my romances of basing my so-called inventions upon a groundwork of actual fact, and of using in their construction methods and materials which are not entirely without the pale of contemporary engineering skill and knowledge.
stops.quote_source: Gordon Jones, 'Jules Verne at Home', Temple Bar, June 1904, vol. 129, p. 670; Verne interviewed in his own house a year before his death
sources: Amiens Tourisme, Maison de Jules Verne
suggested_refs: The house at 44 boulevard Longueville, now boulevard Jules-Verne, Amiens

stops.name: Cimetiere de la Madeleine, the stone broken from inside
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of the monument; the plain slab reading 'Jules Verne 1905' precedes it
stops.campa: The first grave carries a cement slab with a name and a year. In 1907 the family commissions Albert Roze, who had known Verne since the 1890s, and Roze carves a shrouded man tearing his own tombstone open from underneath and reaching upward, the face taken from Verne's death mask. He titles it Vers l'immortalite et l'eternelle jeunesse, a monument unlike any other in the cemetery, where the corpse itself appears to be doing the work of breaking free. Two separate compilations give the cemetery two different wrong coordinates; this is the right one.
stops.quote_source: Title carved for the tomb monument by Albert Roze, Cimetiere de la Madeleine, Amiens, 1907
sources: France 3 Hauts-de-France, 'L'etonnante tombe de Jules Verne'
suggested_refs: Albert Roze's Vers l'immortalite et l'eternelle jeunesse, Cimetiere de la Madeleine

stops.name: Jardin des Plantes, Nantes: the bust that was melted
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day of inauguration
stops.campa: Nantes inaugurates Georges Bareau's monument in the Jardin des Plantes on the twenty-ninth of May, five years after the death. In 1942 the occupying administration requisitions the bronze bust and melts it for metal; a stone bust by Jean Mazuet replaces it in 1945. The monument standing today in his birth city is therefore a replacement carved after a war he did not live to see, on a base laid for an object that was taken away and destroyed. The description of a figure seated on a globe, widely repeated, matches nothing in the sources reached.
sources: audiala.com, Monument a Jules Verne guide
Nantes municipal sources via search summary
suggested_refs: Georges Bareau's 1910 Monument a Jules Verne and Jean Mazuet's 1945 replacement bust

stops.name: Launch Complex 39A, Merritt Island: three men and a Florida gun
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day of the final Apollo 11 telecast; the launch was 16 July 1969
stops.campa: Coming home from the moon, Neil Armstrong opens the last television broadcast by naming a novelist dead sixty-four years. The parallels the newspapers then print are partly wrong: in the 1865 novel the Columbiad is the cannon, not the vehicle, and the launch site is a place Verne calls Tampa Town. What holds is the arithmetic he did at a desk on the Bourse's old hours: three men, a Florida launch, a return that ends in the ocean, and a projectile weight worked out to make the escape velocity come true.
stops.quote: A hundred years ago, Jules Verne wrote a book about a voyage to the moon.
stops.quote_source: Neil Armstrong, opening the final Apollo 11 telecast, 23 July 1969
sources: NASA and space.com summaries of the Apollo 11 Verne references
suggested_refs: The Apollo 11 final telecast transcript, 23 July 1969

stops.name: Butte Sainte-Anne, Nantes: the museum on the hill
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day of inauguration, the 150th anniversary of the birth
stops.campa: The Musee Jules Verne opens at 3 rue de l'Hermitage on the Butte Sainte-Anne, above the Loire and above the quarter where the family took its summer house, on the anniversary of the birth. It arrives late because the reputation arrived late: the English translations from Mercier's 1873 Twenty Thousand Leagues cut up to two fifths of the French and turned a novelist into a writer for boys. In Cordoba, in the early forties, a wheezing schoolboy named Ernesto Guevara reads him with Neruda and Freud, and gets the sea by other means.
stops.quote_source: Walter James Miller, 'The Rehabilitation of Jules Verne in America' (najvs.org), on the gap between the corrupted English author and the French one
sources: Musee Jules Verne, Nantes Metropole official site
suggested_refs: The Musee Jules Verne, 3 rue de l'Hermitage, Nantes, and the Buron house of 1872-78

stops.name: Paris, the safe and the twentieth century
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of French publication; the English translation follows in 1996
stops.campa: Hetzel had refused Paris au XXe siecle around 1863 as too dark and too unsaleable: a future capital of glass towers, gas cars, electric chairs, and a young man who cannot sell a line of poetry and freezes to death. The manuscript goes into a family safe and comes out in 1994. One account has the great-grandson Jean Verne opening the safe in 1989 and discovering it; another holds the location had been known for years and the discovery was a publisher's story. Both are on the record here, and neither is chosen.
suggested_refs: The 1994 Hachette first edition of Paris au XXe siecle
